#### One grouping, two finality rules — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** What the end of an input was doing for a batch job — as one pipeline run in two modes.

`group(events, clock)` is the WHAT and the WHERE, and both modes call it identically with `"et"`. `finalAtBounded` is batch's watermark: it **ignores its argument** and returns 9. That is the trivial-watermark claim made mechanical.

Step 3 is the limit of the convergence — `finalAtStreaming(480)` returns NONE — and step 4 is the historical contrast: the same `group` with `"pt"` differs in the VALUES, 3 of 4 buckets by 26.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch10-history-memory/ch10-history-memory.svg" alt="One grouping, two finality rules — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the grouping is one function, and the clock is its argument</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch10-history-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the grouping is one function, and the clock is its argument" width="980">

`floorTo(e[clock], WIN)` is the whole of WHERE, and `clock` is an argument. Batch and streaming both call this with `"et"` and get the same 4 buckets — the computation was never what distinguished them. Early streaming systems called it with `"pt"` because they had no other option.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — batch's watermark is a constant: end of input</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch10-history-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: batch&#39;s watermark is a constant: end of input" width="980">

It ignores `bucket` entirely and returns 9. That is batch's watermark — the simplest possible one, reaching "everything" at EOF so every window closes together. Batch does not lack a watermark; it has a trivial one, and that is the whole of what an ending buys you.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — streaming asks a real watermark, and one bucket gets NONE</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch10-history-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: streaming asks a real watermark, and one bucket gets NONE" width="980">

The loop runs out: no `watermarkAfter(i)` reaches 600, so bucket 480 returns NONE. Compare the two heap rows — identical window VALUES, and the finality column differs. That difference is the only thing the model does not unify, and it is real: 8 is final in batch and never final in streaming.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the old arrival-time pipeline differs in the VALUES</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch10-history-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the old arrival-time pipeline differs in the VALUES" width="980">

`arrival` is the same function with `"pt"`, and now the VALUES differ, not just the finality: 3 of the 4 buckets, by 26 in total. That is what early streaming systems produced — not an approximation of the batch answer but a different question, because they had no way to name event time.

</details>
